title: Arguments, premises and conclusions
note: In logic, an argument is a set of statements in which some (the premises) are offered as reasons to accept another (the conclusion). Words like 'since' and 'because' often flag premises; 'therefore' and 'so' often flag conclusions. Bare assertions, reports, and explanations of why something happened are not arguments.

read.title: Finding the argument
text: In everyday speech an argument is a fight. In logic it is something calmer: a set of statements where some, the premises, are offered as reasons to believe another, the conclusion. A statement is a sentence that is true or false, so questions and commands are not statements, though a rhetorical question can work like one.

The first job is to locate the conclusion. Ask what the speaker is trying to get you to accept. Indicator words help. 'Therefore', 'so', 'thus', and 'it follows that' tend to come before a conclusion, while 'because', 'since', and 'given that' tend to come before a premise. These words are clues, not proof. 'Because' also appears in explanations, which tell why something we already accept is true rather than trying to show that it is true.

Next, put the argument in standard form: list the premises, draw a line, and write the conclusion beneath. Real arguments often leave a premise unstated. 'Socrates is a man, so he is mortal' depends on the unspoken premise that all men are mortal. Writing such assumptions down makes them easy to inspect, and it is often where the weakness hides.
